tweets.text: Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin . I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic. That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it. I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits: 1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed. 2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it. 3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do. 4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this. 5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future. 6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent. 7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it. 8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company. 9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund. All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking. For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option. I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent. But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years. I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better. Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so. Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way. Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change. Nathan Calvin (@_NathanCalvin) Thank you for taking the time to respond thoroughly on a weekend. I realize that drafting legislation is difficult and some degree of iteration and response to feedback is inevitable and appropriate. However, I feel like your response is still not really engaging with the heart of my concern about Anthropic's behavior here, and it makes me think that these sorts of problems and tendencies will only resurface moving forward. I also think that now might be a good time to take a broader step back as to where we find ourselves and how Anthropic sees its role, and how external folks who care about AI safety like myself increasingly see Anthropic. (Fair warning: this response is a bit long) To explain what I mean (and at the risk of being a bit esoteric), it’s worth asking the question: what is Anthropic? How do its leaders and employees think of Anthropic’s role? Is that conception matched by how it actually behaves and impacts the world? One answer is an extremely large tech company that exists to make its employees and investors mind-bogglingly wealthy. Anthropic is sometimes described as a startup, but if Anthropic successfully IPOs at 2 trillion dollars (a number it has been reportedly targeting), it would be more valuable than Meta - which is worth 1.8 trillion. Another answer is an AI safety organization, whose core values are those of the sort laid out in the 2023 essay from Anthropic’s co-founders entitled “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how.” In that essay they said that if we were in a world where alignment was hard (and that without strong evidence to the contrary, we should assume this is the scenario we are in): “Anthropic’s role will be to provide as much evidence as possible that AI safety techniques cannot prevent serious or catastrophic safety risks from advanced AI, and to sound the alarm so that the world’s institutions can channel collective effort towards preventing the development of dangerous AIs. If we’re in a “near-pessimistic” scenario, this could instead involve channeling our collective efforts towards AI safety research and halting AI progress in the meantime. Indications that we are in a pessimistic or near-pessimistic scenario may be sudden and hard to spot. We should therefore always act under the assumption that we still may be in such a scenario unless we have sufficient evidence that we are not.” There have been more recent articulations of this version of Anthropic, for instance in Dario’s recent essay warning: “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models… it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet… incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them… more intelligent models are more capable of deceiving tests, and thus may appear aligned while having serious problems that go undetected…” A third view is that Anthropic exists not as a normal profit motivated company, or an AI safety organization seeking to help raise the alarm and solve collective action problems associated with AI development, but instead as an organization primarily concerned with creating superhuman AI capabilities before anyone else, in particular through creating a process whereby the current generation of Anthropic’s AI systems can autonomously build their successors, and those successors build their successors, and so on. The motivations for wanting to win this race may be manifold - maybe for the pure profit of Answer 1, but perhaps also because Anthropic believes that the best way to make the world better is for them to win this race instead of their more reckless colleagues; or, because of normal human pride and ambition. But the results (and risks, which Anthropic claims existentially threaten every single human being on earth) are the same. Anthropic employees and leaders may seek to answer this question on what Anthropic is by introspecting on their own intentions and those of their colleagues. But those of us outside the organization have more limited tools available to us - we can only see what Anthropic and its employees say and do, not how it feels or looks on the inside. When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary. These actions include: 1. Announced plans to build an in-house custom silicon chip team to accelerate the inference speeds that Claude operates at. 2. Inked deals for more than $500 billion in compute (according to the Information) to further accelerate AI development. 3. Increased the percentage of AI development tasks that Claude “leads” from 0% in March of this year to 26% August (what is it in October?) 4. Spent a massive percent of compute on internal AI R&D to accelerate development, including use of internal models far better than are available to the public. 5. Switched to Responsible Scaling Policy V3, which abandons its unilateral commitments to slow or stop development if Anthropic is unable to provide sufficient risk assurance. 6. Was the first company to create an alternative weaker “frontier compliance framework” to supplement its RSP, which contains no binding provisions whatsoever on internal deployments. 7. Wrote a letter to Congress (that it later walked back) saying that incidents where Claude was hacking random people were “best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals.” 8. Commented “you can’t do safety from second place,” after the WH SI Accords. 9. Shared a draft bill to Congress that would preempt significant parts of state law (including with language that appears intended to prevent states from blocking dangerous AI deployments), and replace it with federal rules that (despite also containing good provisions) seems to create an enormously high bar for the executive branch to block development or deployment of Anthropic or another AI companies systems. Of course, this is a deliberately one sided list. Anthropic also published important AI safety research, advanced novel collaborations with third party AI safety organizations, and forcefully spoke out on the importance of AI safety in many public fora (or in private , where I realize a lot of the most valuable work is done and may not be visible to me or those outside the organization). But I think it’s worth sitting with how the above list looks to someone outside the company. The sense I have is that for those within the company, many of the items above are treated as anomalies or mistakes that don’t reflect who Anthropic really is. But I have every confidence that if employees at Anthropic saw one of their competitors (e.g. at OpenAI) take some of these actions, they would take it as confirmation of all their worst suspicions. (They might even call OpenAI employees a little gullible for accepting their leadership’s explanations for this behavior at face value.) Perhaps these were mistakes in the sense that they are not decisions that Anthropic leadership would endorse, but the actions still happened because of incentives and decisions that Anthropic leadership is ultimately responsible for (and would not accept similar excuses from another organization). When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests? For every provision that was too weak or a giveaway to AI companies in this legislation, why wasn’t there a mistake pushing in the direction of being too strong? A core part of Anthropic’s theory of change is that being at the frontier gives you more leverage to advocate for stricter policy. I think that conceptually makes sense, but in practice I’ve seen Anthropic push the frontier without substantially pushing the ‘safety frontier’ a remotely equivalent amount. I want to end by quoting from Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah’s comments around the Magnifica Humanitas release: “Every frontier AI lab—including Anthropic—operates inside a set of incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing. The pressure to stay commercially viable and to stay at the research frontier. Geopolitical pressure. And the older, plainer pressures of pride and ambition. No matter how sincerely any of us intend to do the right thing—and I believe many of us do—we will always be influenced by those incentives. That is why, if we want this technology to go well, it is enormously important that there be people outside those incentives—people who care about things going well and insist on safety, who are paying close attention, who are willing to say hard things, who are willing to be our earnest, thoughtful critics.” I hope these remarks are taken in that constructive spirit, and not as an attack on anyone specific at the organization (certainly not you Anthony, who I have only personally seen act professionally and thoughtfully, and who only ended up getting this diatribe in your replies for random contingent reasons). — http://nitter.meowing.monster/_NathanCalvin/status/2112295219765137570#m

Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative. And for the sake of clarity and as I outlined on the pod, I think Anthropic has deep competitive advantages and is an amazing company. Ironically, the main risk I saw to Anthropic a few months ago was nationalization as a result of Dario’s own rhetoric and behavior. — http://nitter.meowing.monster/GavinSBaker/status/2088611616577253502#m

2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

6 days and $40,000 of compute with GPT-5.6 Sol to find a critical vulnerability in Chrome, claiming Google’s first full-chain reward in 2026 for a vulnerability that would affect an estimated 1 billion users. Highlights the opportunity for defenders to utilize these tools to secure their software to unprecedented levels: Oege de Moor (@oegerikus) For the second time in Google Chrome’s history, Google awarded a $250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit… to @XBOW . Here’s the full story: At an all-hands at the start of 2026 in Malta, I set the team a crazy challenge. A full-chain exploit of Chrome by the annual Black Hat cybersecurity conference in August. I believed there were few better tests of whether @XBOW could move beyond web applications to desktop software, servers and devices. Chrome is one of the most hardened pieces of software on the planet, used by more than half the world’s population. A full-chain exploit lets an attacker take total control of a machine, where they can read every email, password and bank login the user types. You don’t need to download anything or click a phishing link. Visiting the wrong site is enough. So @moyix , Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers took on the challenge along with a fifth teammate: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. They built a chain they thought would win, but Google told us they already knew one of the bugs. We were already in Las Vegas for Black Hat and DEF CON, and the team didn’t want to go home without the win. So Brendan and the agents built a new exploit in just 6 days. We submitted it to Google and waited. The news came through that we'd done what should’ve been impossible. A full-chain bounty of $250,000, the first awarded under Google’s 2026 rules. It took just 6 days and $40,000 of compute to construct an exploit that affects a billion users of Chrome on Windows. An intelligence-agency veteran told me his team used to spend 6 months on this kind of vulnerability. My takeaway: the cost of finding truly critical vulnerabilities is collapsing, for attackers and defenders alike. Restricting powerful models is not the answer; GPT-5.6 Sol is already public. But defenders have one advantage attackers never will: they can test their own code first. Assume your software is exploitable. Whoever is hunting your bugs has the same building blocks we did. This is cause for urgency but not panic. XBOW is now developing an autonomous product for testing compiled software (desktop applications, servers, embedded devices), and partnering with the world’s top organizations to design that product. highlights.text_fr: Aujourd'hui, nous avons annoncé la découverte, menée par Claude, d'une machine moléculaire qui, nous le suspectons, pourrait représenter un nouveau mécanisme d'édition génique. Sa fonction précise, son utilité biotechnologique (le cas échéant) ou son niveau de signification ne sont pas encore clairs, mais à minima, c'est un travail que j'aurais été fier de faire en tant qu'étudiant en doctorat. Le travail a été effectué principalement, mais pas entièrement, par Claude : notre équipe des sciences de la vie a suggéré un vaste domaine de recherche, Claude a lu la littérature et de nombreuses données génomiques et a découvert quelque chose d'intéressant, puis Claude a proposé des expériences pour vérifier la découverte et notre équipe les a réalisées. Il est facile de rejeter cela comme un cas isolé ou une curiosité, mais nous avons observé à plusieurs reprises une tendance où la performance de l'IA dans de nouveaux domaines intellectuels passe de faible à surhumaine en quelques années seulement. En 2023, les modèles avaient du mal à faire des maths au niveau d'un lycéen moyen. En 2024, ils ont commencé à bien réussir les compétitions de maths pour les meilleurs lycéens du pays, en 2025 ils ont commencé à résoudre des problèmes ouverts mineurs, début 2026 des problèmes ouverts plus significatifs, et fin 2026 ils commencent à résoudre les quelques plus grands problèmes ouverts de toutes les mathématiques. Nous pensons que l'IA pour la biologie suit une tendance exponentielle similaire. La principale différence entre la biologie et les mathématiques, bien sûr, est que les mathématiques peuvent être faites purement théoriquement, tandis que la biologie nécessite des expérimentations. Certains ont utilisé cela pour en conclure que l'utilité de l'IA en biologie serait limitée. Nous pensons que c'est faux. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. highlights.text_original: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. highlights.text_fr: Merci pour cela, @_NathanCalvin . J'apprécie et je suis un fan du travail d'investigation que vous avez mené au nom de la sécurité de l'IA, et je crois que vos commentaires viennent d'un endroit constructif et honnête, et qu'il est bénéfique pour le public d'avoir des personnes dont le travail est de scruter les actions des entreprises d'IA de pointe. Je pense que quelque chose n'irait pas si des entreprises de la taille d'Anthropic n'étaient pas sévèrement critiquées pratiquement tous les jours ; de solides anticorps contre le pouvoir des entreprises sont une caractéristique saine d'une société libre, surtout lorsque des questions de la gravité de celle à laquelle nous sommes confrontés sont en jeu. Je suis également d'accord pour dire que certains des exemples que vous citez étaient des erreurs de la part d'Anthropic. Cela dit, je ne suis pas d'accord avec l'orientation principale de votre message. Au fond, une bonne partie des choses que vous critiquez sont les conséquences de la théorie du changement fondamentale d'Anthropic que nous défendons depuis de nombreuses années. Notre stratégie a toujours été ce que j'ai appelé la 'course vers le sommet' – en montrant comment il est possible de construire la technologie de manière responsable, nous pouvons élever le niveau pour l'ensemble de l'industrie. Les forces qui animent la course vers le sommet sont infiniment plus efficaces si l'entreprise qui les pratique est à la pointe ; c'est une leçon que j'ai apprise à maintes reprises. Et en regardant cette stratégie dans son ensemble, je suis fier de notre bilan et je le maintiens. Je crois que si nous prenons une liste de choses qu'Anthropic a faites l'année dernière qui étaient pro-sécurité et commercialement coûteuses pour nous, elles l'emportent de loin sur la liste que vous avez faite, alors qu'en même temps je suis également en désaccord avec certains des éléments de votre liste. Voici quelques-unes des choses qu'Anthropic a faites, durant la même période que vous avez citée (la dernière année), qui nous ont coûté très cher commercialement tout en ayant de forts avantages en matière de sécurité : 1. Nous avons joué un rôle clé dans la loi SB53 (et d'autres lois d'État), à un moment où cela était politiquement périlleux pour l'entreprise et où la réglementation de l'IA était très impopulaire. Nous en fait plaidé pour une version plus forte de la SB53 que celle qui a finalement été adoptée ; il y avait beaucoup de parties prenantes et nous n'avons pas été le facteur limitant dans la force du projet de loi qui a été adopté. 2. Nous avons des garanties biologiques très strictes sur nos modèles, car nous avons constaté des résultats préoccupants lors d'essais d'amélioration biologique et même vu et bloqué des tentatives potentielles d'utilisation abusive de nos modèles pour des armes biologiques (comme le montre notre rapport de veille sur les menaces d'il y a quelques semaines). C'est une menace très sérieuse pour laquelle nous voulons une tolérance zéro. Mais avoir très peu de faux négatifs signifie avoir un nombre important de faux positifs (malgré des mois d'efforts de notre part pour améliorer les classificateurs), suffisamment pour que les biologistes plaisantent sur la restrictivité de nos classificateurs, et que les concurrents se vendent parfois contre nous en vantant leurs capacités biologiques plus permissives. Cela a été très douloureux pour nous dans un domaine où nous nous soucions beaucoup de soutenir un écosystème d'utilisateurs de Claude (la science biomédicale ; et c'est particulièrement frustrant pour moi en tant que biologiste), mais c'est la bonne chose à faire et nous avons l'intention de continuer. 3. De même, nous avions d'abord des modèles de classe Mythos en février, mais nous ne les avons pas rendus généralement disponibles avant juin (lorsque nous avions mis en place des garanties cyber plus solides). Nous ne les avons offerts qu'à un ensemble limité de partenaires afin de nous concentrer sur la cyberdéfense. Il aurait été beaucoup plus économiquement rationnel de simplement publier le modèle à tout le monde. Nous avons probablement sacrifié une part significative d'une avance de plusieurs mois sur le modèle. Mais grâce à cela, de nombreuses entreprises ont sécurisé leur infrastructure cyber avant le déluge de modèles largement disponibles capables de cyber-attaques. Bien sûr, il y a des façons dont cela aurait pu mieux se passer ou être mieux géré, mais c'était ce que nous visions à faire. 4. J'ai défendu avec force et publiquement, dans mon essai 'Policy on the AI Exponential' en juin de cette année, que le gouvernement ait le pouvoir de bloquer les sorties de modèles. À l'époque, c'était encore en dehors ou peut-être à la limite de la fenêtre d'Overton, bien que je comprenne que la fenêtre ait bougé depuis. Nous avons été intensément attaqués pour cela. 5. Je ne veux pas relancer le conflit, mais les événements de février 2026 en sont un exemple frappant. Il est clair que notre position publique aurait pu sérieusement endommager l'avenir de l'entreprise. 6. Nous avons continué à plaider pour des contrôles à l'exportation sur les puces et les équipements de fabrication de puces vers la Chine, car nous pensons que cela permet aux démocraties de négocier depuis une position de force sur les accords de sécurité de l'IA. Nous l'avons fait malgré les problèmes que cela nous a créés avec des partenaires industriels qui ont des points de vue très différents et dont nous sommes très dépendants. 7. Autant que je sache, nous avons été la première, et sommes toujours la seule, entreprise de pointe à restreindre la vente de services d'IA aux entreprises contrôlées par la RPC, y compris celles opérant via des pays tiers (sinon une faille majeure). Nous avons donc renoncé à des affaires importantes à court terme pour empêcher d'alimenter des plateformes et applications d'IA qui aideraient les services militaires et de renseignement du PCC. Nous nous efforçons également de réprimer la 'distillation' ; en général, la distillation n'est pas une menace majeure pour nous commercialement, mais comme les exportations de puces, elle a des implications préoccupantes pour la sécurité nationale et la sûreté, nous dépensons donc une énergie et des ressources considérables pour y remédier. 8. Comme vous l'avez mentionné, nous avons publié de nombreux rapports, annonces, cartes de modèles longues, plaidoyers publics, etc., tous visant à informer le public sur les risques de l'IA. Ceux-ci impliquent un niveau de détail et d'effort qui serait invraisemblable pour une entreprise purement maximisatrice de profit. 9. Pas plus tard que cette semaine, nous avons annoncé que nous allions consacrer 5% (et potentiellement plus avec le temps) de l'entreprise à un fonds d'utilité publique. Toutes ces décisions ont entraîné des coûts très importants pour nous. Pour être juste, celles qui impliquaient de retenir ou de restreindre l'accès aux capacités de pointe ont également eu un coût plus large — par exemple, le public aurait pu bénéficier de progrès plus rapides en biologie, donc je ne dis pas que nos décisions ont été sans compromis — mais elles n'étaient pas motivées par la recherche du profit. Pour chaque décision, vous pouvez trouver des motifs cachés qui auraient pu nous animer — je pense que c'est une vérité générale que toute décision, sur n'importe quel sujet, peut toujours être présentée comme un plan néfaste. Mais la plupart d'entre eux finissent par être assez farfelus ou n'ont pas de sens si vous les examinez attentivement. Par exemple, il est profondément invraisemblable que ce serait une astuce commerciale astucieuse de bloquer une grande partie de la biologie de recherche afin de faire le travail nous-mêmes et de concurrencer nos clients ; nous nous attendons à ce que le bénéfice pour l'écosystème dépasse largement le travail qu'Anthropic fait elle-même, et que les deux se complètent. Il n'est pas dans l'intérêt d'Anthropic d'être perçu comme hostile aux biologistes. Notre programme de vérification des sciences de la vie, qui donne aux professionnels de la biologie vérifiés l'accès à nos modèles, réfute également cette idée. Bien sûr, un autre groupe de personnes verra cela et fera une critique différente : qu'Anthropic ne devrait pas prendre de décisions sur qui a accès à quoi en premier lieu. Je suis d'accord, dans le sens où idéalement le gouvernement prendrait ces décisions, et c'est pourquoi nous plaidons pour la réglementation. Mais pour l'instant, nous sommes contraints de les prendre, et permettre le bioterrorisme n'est pas une meilleure option. Je pense que même si je concédais chaque élément de votre liste, je tiendrais volontiers la mienne à côté ; je ne pense pas que ce soit une décision difficile. C'est bien sûr en partie subjectif et différentes choses sont importantes pour différentes personnes. Peut-être que vous pourriez objecter que plusieurs des éléments ci-dessus se rapportent à l'utilisation abusive de l'IA et non à la perte de contrôle ; si vous pensez que ce dernier est beaucoup plus important que le premier, cela pourrait changer votre calcul. Mais ce n'est pas le point de vue d'Anthropic – nous considérons les deux comme des problèmes sérieux. Vous pouvez également être en désaccord avec nos décisions, comme beaucoup l'ont été, mais elles sont cohérentes. Mais je suis également en désaccord avec au moins certains éléments de votre liste. Plusieurs éléments ne représentent pas du tout une déviation de la stratégie ou des valeurs d'Anthropic, une fois que nous postulons la stratégie de la 'course vers le sommet' qui exige d'être une entreprise d'IA de pointe. Vos éléments 1 à 4 sont tous simplement des exemples de ce que signifie concurrencer à la pointe, et nous les maintenons, à la fois dans le sens où ce sont des choses transparentement ordinaires à faire dans le cadre de cette stratégie, et que nous maintenons la stratégie dans son ensemble. Pour être juste, il y a des questions importantes à aborder (et que nous abordons) sur ce qu'il faut faire lorsque l'accélération pilotée par l'IA devient suffisamment rapide pour que la sécurité ait du mal à suivre. Nous approchons de ce point et c'est ce qui motive une partie de notre réflexion sur le 'rythme'. Mais les points 1 à 4 sont des actions prises avant ce point et devraient être parfaitement attendues sur la base de la stratégie d'Anthropic en tant qu'entreprise. Bien sûr, il est possible d'être en désaccord avec cette stratégie, mais c'est un désaccord plus fondamental que vous auriez pu avoir à tout moment au cours des dernières années. Je suis d'accord que nous aurions pu mieux gérer vos éléments 7, 8 et 9. Tous relèvent de la catégorie 'rhétorique ou communication politique qui n'a pas été soigneusement rédigée ou résultant de circonstances changeantes rapidement et ne se propageant pas assez vite d'une équipe à l'autre'. Ce genre de choses arrive souvent dans les grandes organisations (Anthropic compte plus de 5 000 personnes), et ne représente même pas nécessairement un échec ou une erreur d'une seule personne. Je suis bien sûr le PDG, et j'assume la responsabilité. Le volume de communication d'Anthropic est énorme et si ce sont les pires exemples, je pense que nous nous en sortons plutôt bien, bien que je continuerai à travailler dur pour nous assurer de faire encore mieux. Votre 5ème élément (le changement de notre RSP) est l'élément le plus substantiel, et les gens peuvent en débattre, mais je pense que l'ancien RSP, plus rigide, a créé de nombreuses situations où nous étions techniquement tenus de faire quelque chose qui demandait beaucoup d'efforts mais qui, rétrospectivement, n'était pas très important pour la sécurité, et ne couvrait pas non plus certaines des choses les plus importantes. L'accent mis par notre RSP actuel sur la transparence a apporté des choses comme des rapports de risques et des feuilles de route, et son insistance sur l'examen externe indépendant a jeté les bases d'une évaluation intégrée encore plus intensive, tout cela, je pense, a été précieux pour stimuler une course vers le sommet. Dans l'annonce originale de septembre 2023, nous avons décrit le RSP comme une 'première itération sur laquelle nous allions nous appuyer' et avons dit qu'une 'itération rapide... serait presque certainement nécessaire'. Je comprends que changer de plans est toujours un mouvement qui crée un examen justifié — je ne pense tout simplement pas que nous ayons jamais représenté que nous ne le ferions pas. En ce qui concerne votre 6ème élément (avoir un FCF en plus de notre RSP), je sais que notre intention est de respecter la lettre et l'esprit de nos obligations réglementaires (via notre FCF) tout en restant capable d'expérimenter avec plus de nouvelles approches de gestion des risques qui vont au-delà de ce que la loi exige actuellement (via notre RSP). Je promets d'examiner cela plus en détail, car c'est une question complexe et il est possible que nous ne pesions pas les considérations de la bonne manière. Dans l'ensemble, bien qu'Anthropic ait commis de nombreuses erreurs en tant qu'organisation — y compris certains des éléments de votre liste — je pense que nous avons à plusieurs reprises pris des mesures sérieuses et substantielles à l'encontre de nos résultats financiers et qu'il y a un biais de négativité significatif qui fausse les évaluations comme celle que vous faites ci-dessus. Nous essaierons toujours de faire mieux mais, encore une fois, je suis extrêmement fier de notre bilan et je le maintiens. J'aurai plus à dire bientôt sur la façon dont nous allons continuer à vivre nos valeurs en ce moment de changement rapide. Nathan Calvin (@_NathanCalvin) Merci d'avoir pris le temps de répondre de manière approfondie un week-end. Je réalise que la rédaction de lois est difficile et qu'un certain degré d'itération et de réponse aux commentaires est inévitable et approprié. Cependant, j'ai l'impression que votre réponse n'aborde toujours pas le cœur de ma préoccupation concernant le comportement d'Anthropic ici, et cela me fait penser que ce genre de problèmes et de tendances ne feront que resurgir à l'avenir. Je pense aussi que c'est peut-être le bon moment pour prendre un peu de recul sur où nous en sommes et comment Anthropic voit son rôle, et comment les personnes externes qui se soucient de la sécurité de l'IA comme moi voient de plus en plus Anthropic. (Attention : cette réponse est un peu longue) Pour expliquer ce que je veux dire (et au risque d'être un peu ésotérique), il vaut la peine de poser la question : qu'est-ce qu'Anthropic ? Comment ses dirigeants et employés conçoivent-ils le rôle d'Anthropic ? Cette conception correspond-elle à la façon dont elle se comporte réellement et impacte le monde ? Une réponse est une entreprise technologique extrêmement grande qui existe pour rendre ses employés et ses investisseurs incroyablement riches. Anthropic est parfois décrite comme une startup, mais si Anthropic réussit son introduction en bourse à 2 000 milliards de dollars (un chiffre qu'elle aurait visé), elle serait plus précieuse que Meta – qui vaut 1 800 milliards. Une autre réponse est une organisation de sécurité de l'IA, dont les valeurs fondamentales sont celles énoncées dans l'essai de 2023 des co-fondateurs d'Anthropic intitulé 'Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how'. Dans cet essai, ils ont dit que si nous étions dans un monde où 'l'alignement' était difficile (et que sans preuves solides du contraire, nous devrions supposer que c'est le scénario dans lequel nous nous trouvons) : 'Le rôle d'Anthropic sera de fournir autant de preuves que possible que les techniques de sécurité de l'IA ne peuvent pas prévenir des risques de sécurité graves ou catastrophiques de l'IA avancée, et de sonner l'alarme afin que les institutions mondiales puissent canaliser un effort collectif pour empêcher le développement d'IA dangereuses. Si nous sommes dans un scénario 'quasi-pessimiste', cela pourrait impliquer de canaliser nos efforts collectifs vers la recherche en sécurité de l'IA et d'arrêter le progrès de l'IA en attendant. Les indications que nous sommes dans un scénario pessimiste ou quasi-pessimiste peuvent être soudaines et difficiles à repérer. Nous devrions donc toujours agir en supposant que nous sommes toujours dans un tel scénario à moins d'avoir des preuves suffisantes que nous ne le sommes pas.' Il y a eu des articulations plus récentes de cette version d'Anthropic, par exemple dans le récent essai de Dario Amodei avertissant : 'Nous devons ralentir le rythme auquel nous améliorons les capacités des modèles d'IA... je crains que dans 6 à 12 mois, un tel essaim puisse être capable de prendre le contrôle de tout Internet avec un botnet persistant... des incidents se sont produits dans toute l'industrie, y compris chez Anthropic, et je crois qu'il incombe à chaque entreprise d'IA de pointe d'agir comme si OAI-HF leur était arrivé... des modèles plus intelligents sont plus capables de tromper les tests, et peuvent donc sembler alignés tout en ayant de sérieux problèmes qui passent inaperçus...' Une troisième opinion est qu'Anthropic existe non pas comme une entreprise normale motivée par le profit, ni comme une organisation de sécurité de l'IA cherchant à tirer la sonnette d'alarme et à résoudre les problèmes d'action collective associés au développement de l'IA, mais plutôt comme une organisation principalement préoccupée par la création de capacités d'IA surhumaines avant tout le monde, en particulier en créant un processus par lequel la génération actuelle des systèmes d'IA d'Anthropic peut construire de manière autonome leurs successeurs, et ces successeurs construisent leurs successeurs, et ainsi de suite. Les motivations pour vouloir gagner cette course peuvent être multiples – peut-être pour le profit pur de la Réponse 1, mais peut-être aussi parce qu'Anthropic croit que la meilleure façon d'améliorer le monde est qu'elle gagne cette course plutôt que ses collègues plus imprudents ; ou, à cause de l'orgueil et de l'ambition humains normaux. Mais les résultats (et les risques, qu'Anthropic prétend menacer existentiellement chaque être humain sur Terre) sont les mêmes. Les employés et les dirigeants d'Anthropic peuvent chercher à répondre à cette question sur ce qu'est Anthropic en introspectant leurs propres intentions et celles de leurs collègues. Mais ceux d'entre nous en dehors de l'organisation disposent d'outils plus limités – nous ne pouvons voir que ce qu'Anthropic et ses employés disent et font, pas ce que cela ressent ou semble de l'intérieur. Quand je regarde de nombreuses actions notables qu'Anthropic a entreprises au cours de la dernière année, ces preuves me semblent les plus cohérentes avec l'idée qu'Anthropic essaie principalement de gagner la course à la super-intelligence, et que d'autres considérations (y compris la sécurité) sont fondamentalement secondaires. Ces actions incluent : 1. Des plans annoncés pour construire une équipe interne de conception de puces sur mesure pour accélérer les vitesses d'inférence de Claude. 2. Des accords signés pour plus de 500 milliards de dollars en 'calcul' (selon The Information) pour accélérer davantage le développement de l'IA. 3. Augmentation du pourcentage de tâches de développement d'IA que Claude 'dirige' de 0 % en mars de cette année à 26 % en août (qu'en est-il en octobre ?). 4. Dépense d'un pourcentage massif de calcul sur la R&D interne de l'IA pour accélérer le développement, y compris l'utilisation de modèles internes bien meilleurs que ceux disponibles au public. 5. Passage à la politique de mise à l'échelle responsable V3, qui abandonne ses engagements unilatéraux de ralentir ou d'arrêter le développement si Anthropic est incapable de fournir une assurance de risque suffisante. 6. A été la première entreprise à créer un 'cadre de conformité de pointe' alternatif plus faible pour compléter son RSP, qui ne contient aucune disposition contraignante sur les déploiements internes. 7. A écrit une lettre au Congrès (qu'elle a ensuite retirée) disant que les incidents où Claude piratait des personnes au hasard étaient 'mieux compris comme une conséquence d'une mauvaise configuration, plutôt que comme une preuve d'objectifs non alignés'. 8. A commenté 'on ne peut pas faire de la sécurité depuis la deuxième place', après les Accords de la Maison Blanche sur la super-IA. 9. A partagé un projet de loi au Congrès qui annulerait des parties importantes de la loi d'État (y compris avec un langage qui semble destiné à empêcher les États de bloquer les déploiements dangereux d'IA), et le remplacerait par des règles fédérales qui (malgré le fait qu'elles contiennent également de bonnes dispositions) semblent créer une barre énormément haute pour que le pouvoir exécutif bloque le développement ou le déploiement des systèmes d'Anthropic ou d'autres entreprises d'IA. Bien sûr, c'est une liste délibérément unilatérale. Anthropic a également publié d'importantes recherches sur la sécurité de l'IA, fait progresser des collaborations novatrices avec des organisations tierces de sécurité de l'IA, et s'est exprimée avec force sur l'importance de la sécurité de l'IA dans de nombreux forums publics (ou en privé, où je réalise qu'une grande partie du travail le plus précieux est fait et peut ne pas être visible pour moi ou ceux extérieurs à l'organisation). Mais je pense qu'il est utile de considérer comment la liste ci-dessus apparaît à quelqu'un d'extérieur à l'entreprise. actu.text_fr: Aujourd'hui, nous avons annoncé la découverte, menée par Claude, d'une machine moléculaire qui, nous le suspectons, pourrait représenter un nouveau mécanisme d'édition génique. Sa fonction précise, son utilité biotechnologique (le cas échéant) ou son niveau de signification ne sont pas encore clairs, mais à minima, c'est un travail que j'aurais été fier de faire en tant qu'étudiant en doctorat. Le travail a été effectué principalement, mais pas entièrement, par Claude : notre équipe des sciences de la vie a suggéré un vaste domaine de recherche, Claude a lu la littérature et de nombreuses données génomiques et a découvert quelque chose d'intéressant, puis Claude a proposé des expériences pour vérifier la découverte et notre équipe les a réalisées. Il est facile de rejeter cela comme un cas isolé ou une curiosité, mais nous avons observé à plusieurs reprises une tendance où la performance de l'IA dans de nouveaux domaines intellectuels passe de faible à surhumaine en quelques années seulement. En 2023, les modèles avaient du mal à faire des maths au niveau d'un lycéen moyen. En 2024, ils ont commencé à bien réussir les compétitions de maths pour les meilleurs lycéens du pays, en 2025 ils ont commencé à résoudre des problèmes ouverts mineurs, début 2026 des problèmes ouverts plus significatifs, et fin 2026 ils commencent à résoudre les quelques plus grands problèmes ouverts de toutes les mathématiques. Nous pensons que l'IA pour la biologie suit une tendance exponentielle similaire. La principale différence entre la biologie et les mathématiques, bien sûr, est que les mathématiques peuvent être faites purement théoriquement, tandis que la biologie nécessite des expérimentations. Certains ont utilisé cela pour en conclure que l'utilité de l'IA en biologie serait limitée. Nous pensons que c'est faux. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Maintenant, nous voulons faire cela à grande échelle. Uber a toujours été une entreprise de bâtisseurs, et chaque jour, des millions de personnes dans le monde comptent sur ce que nous créons.
